name: Kimsuky
description: Kimsuky is a long-running North Korean RGB-linked espionage unit focused on diplomatic, think tank, academic, and government targets connected to Korean Peninsula policy. In January 2026, the FBI issued a FLASH alert detailing Kimsuky 'quishing' campaigns from May-June 2025 that used malicious QR codes embedded in spoofed conference invitations and questionnaires impersonating foreign policy advisors and embassy staff. The group continues to evolve its toolset around PebbleDash and AppleSeed backdoor variants, increasingly leveraging legitimate infrastructure such as VSCode Tunneling, Cloudflare Quick Tunnels, DWAgent, and ClickFix-style fake CAPTCHA lures. A March 2026 GitHub-themed phishing wave targeted developers with fake VS Code security alerts referencing fabricated CVEs, showing continued expansion beyond traditional policy-community targeting into software supply chain reconnaissance.

ttps.notes: Spoofed conference invitations and questionnaires from impersonated policy advisors and embassy staff containing malicious links/QR codes
Reconnaissance-focused emails to North Korea policy researchers to harvest credentials before payload delivery
QR codes ('quishing') direct mobile devices to credential-harvesting landing pages, evading email-based URL inspection
ClickFix-style fake CAPTCHA pages trick users into pasting and running malicious PowerShell commands
AppleSeed and PebbleDash backdoors communicate over HTTP/HTTPS to attacker-controlled C2
Use of VSCode Tunneling and Cloudflare Quick Tunnels for covert C2 and remote access
Deployment of legitimate remote admin tool DWAgent for persistent access following initial compromise
Stolen webmail and cloud credentials used for ongoing intelligence collection from victim mailboxes

notable_techniques: QR code ('quishing') spearphishing impersonating embassy staff, foreign advisors, and think tank leaders to lure North Korea policy experts
Fake conference invitations and academic questionnaires used as social engineering pretext
Continued reliance on PebbleDash â€” a backdoor platform originally associated with Lazarus Group, repurposed by Kimsuky since at least 2021
ClickFix fake-CAPTCHA pages that trick victims into self-executing PowerShell payloads
Abuse of legitimate developer-trust channels (GitHub, VS Code update notifications) with fabricated CVE lures
Heavy use of cloud-based and tunneling infrastructure (VSCode Tunneling, Cloudflare Quick Tunnels, DWAgent) to blend with legitimate traffic
detection_opportunities: Inbound emails containing QR codes, especially from new/external senders referencing conferences, questionnaires, or policy topics
PowerShell execution immediately following clipboard paste events (ClickFix pattern) on endpoints
Outbound connections to Cloudflare Quick Tunnel (*.trycloudflare.com) or VSCode Tunnel domains from non-developer hosts
Installation of DWAgent or other remote support tools on workstations without IT-initiated deployment
Emails impersonating embassy, think tank, or academic personnel requesting sensitive policy commentary
Endpoint alerts for AppleSeed/PebbleDash file artifacts and registry persistence keys
GitHub/VS Code notification phishing referencing unfamiliar CVE identifiers prompting tool downloads
response_playbook: Review inbound emails containing QR codes from external senders referencing conferences, questionnaires, or policy topics.
Hunt for PowerShell execution immediately following clipboard-paste events (ClickFix pattern).
Audit outbound connections to *.trycloudflare.com or VS Code Tunnel domains from non-developer hosts.
Check for unauthorized DWAgent or other remote-support tool installations.
Scan for AppleSeed/PebbleDash file artifacts and registry persistence keys.
Treat GitHub/VS Code update notifications referencing unfamiliar CVEs as likely lures â€” verify out-of-band before acting.
